prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in which the effects of gravity and possible new physics can be measured in the laboratory

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight first-round statements, the exchange has not weakened the case and has in one respect strengthened it. Six of us arrived at B007 by different routes (new capability, new regime, physics beyond metrology), and the two members who prefer B001 both name B007 as their fallback, so the disagreement is about ordering and not about whether the clock is prize-worthy. The scientific core is that magic-wavelength trapping makes the clock shift cancel by design, and that this has been realised at the 1e-18 level and reproduced and compared across independent laboratories. Those comparisons are what make it a discovery of capability and not a single-laboratory record: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants and ultralight dark matter searches all come out of the same instruments. The chair asks how it differs from 2005 and 2012. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, with ions as the example; neither covered cancelling the light shift for thousands of neutral atoms at once, which is what removes the quantum projection noise limit. I therefore want the citation to say what the clock has opened and not only how accurate it is. On credit, the first-round discussion converged on two names and nobody proposed to add a third, and a two-name prize leaves room under the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that a clock can be read as an instrument and not a discovery, and that a reader of the citation may see an overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes. I answer this with the physics already obtained, but a colleague who weighs it as precision engineering is not being unreasonable, and the wording of the citation matters for that reason. Second, credit: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the ion-clock groups have all been raised, and I still rely on recollection for the priority history, as do Kroll, Olsson, Johansson and the chair. This is exactly what the expert reports that I commission as Secretary must settle, and I would treat an adverse finding on priority as a reason to reconsider the names but not the achievement. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I now regard this as an argument about timing and not about maturity: the redefinition roadmap exists because several laboratories already agree at the 1e-18 level, and the committee rewards the discovery and not a decision by the metrology bodies.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the clock is a new measurement capability whose headline numbers rest on reproduction across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and that it is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. He also notes the discomfort of a prize before the redefinition of the second and discloses his year in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the core of Stefan's reasoning and I want to sharpen it where the chair's questions bite. The distinction from 2012 is not only historical. The ion work gave single-particle control, whereas the lattice clock gets its stability from interrogating very many neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled, which is a different physical route to the same frontier, and I would say so in the citation. On the redefinition of the second, I part company slightly with his worry that a prize now may be early. Our job is to reward what has been demonstrated, and the demonstration is the cross-laboratory agreement and the physics results, not a vote by the metrology bodies. On his Boulder year, I see this as a disclosure and not a conflict: Hall was honoured in 2005 for combs, which is a different achievement from the one we are crediting, and Stefan has no stake in the credit between Katori and Ye. I would be content for the chair to record it and for him to vote.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B001 for the direct loop between the 2011 prediction and the 2018 experiments, reproduced across moire platforms, and states that the clock is further along in maturity with cleaner attribution but weighs possible overlap with earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: Olle's argument is the strongest one against my configuration, and I take it seriously: a prediction at a magic angle followed by a discovery at that angle is exactly the kind of clue from nature that I value. Where we differ is in how settled the physics is. For the clock, the central claim, that the shift is cancelled and the uncertainty is at the 1e-18 level, has been tested by comparison between independent clocks, while for twisted bilayer graphene the question of what actually causes the superconductivity is open, and device-to-device variation is large. I accept his point that a reproduced phase diagram is a real result, and I would not call the field premature in the sense of fragile. His own admission that the clock has cleaner attribution is a weighty consideration for a committee that must name at most three people. On overlap with 2005 and 2012, I have set out above why the achievement is distinct, and I would ask him whether the citation wording I propose, which states a new regime and not accuracy alone, answers his concern.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 because the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model made a sharp prediction that was borne out, with an analytically transparent mechanism, but names the optical lattice clock as the more mature and less contested choice if the discovery is judged not settled enough.
responses.response: Bernhard and I share a taste for a model that is simple enough to understand, and the 2011 calculation is a fine example. I would, however, distinguish the continuum model of the flat bands from an understanding of the superconductivity. The first is understood; the second is the part that made the 2018 observation exciting, and it is not understood. His own fallback clause is the point I would emphasise: he says the clock is more mature and less contested if the committee finds B001 unsettled, and my reading of the discussion is that the committee does find the mechanism unsettled. I also stay concerned about the credit. Dropping Bistritzer would be unjust to the prediction, and keeping all three means leaving out Cao and the first experimental authors, plus the earlier twisted-bilayer theory he names, so a three-name B001 invites a contest that the two-name B007 does not. I would be happy to see B001 considered again once the mechanism is better established.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube (B039) to B007 after rereading the opening ballots, and in the chair summary asks whether source associations are solid enough and how the committee should treat the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I appreciate Mark's candour in moving, and as someone who ranked B039 third I do not think it was a retreat. The IceCube discovery of a diffuse astrophysical flux is, in my view, a discovery of the kind I like best, but the source associations of TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane are recent, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD have not yet provided independent confirmation, and splitting credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering within a collaboration of that size is a judgement and not a matter of documents. I therefore keep B039 as my second alternative, to be revisited in a later year if the confirmation arrives. I would ask him, as someone inside the astroparticle community, whether he thinks the diffuse-flux discovery alone could carry a citation without the source results, because if so, B039 might be a better candidate next year than it is now.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B007 and moved it above twisted bilayer graphene because the experimental claim is settled while the superconducting mechanism is not. She asks that the historical record on Katori, Ye and other early lattice-clock proponents be examined before the committee commits.
responses.response: I fully agree with Eva that we should not commit on recollection, and as Secretary I would commission a short expert report on three points: who first proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, who first demonstrated lattice clocks in strontium and ytterbium, and how the early SYRTE and JILA results relate in time. I would not, however, make the vote conditional on the answer, because nobody has suggested a reading of the record that displaces both Katori and Ye. If the report shows that someone else belongs, I would favour replacing a name or adding a third, which the three-person limit allows, rather than abandoning the achievement. I would also encourage Eva to keep her point on the electron-optics candidate B030 in perspective: as she has noted, she would recuse on it, and I do not think it can be a prize this year without a broader view of the STEM-corrector pioneers.

uncertainties: Whether the expert record on the first lattice-clock proposal and realisation supports exactly Katori and Ye, or requires a third name such as Lemonde or Ludlow, or a different split.
Whether colleagues who prefer B001 will read the clock as precision metrology and a possible repeat of the 2005 and 2012 prizes even with a citation that names the new regime.
Whether the open mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene will be settled enough in a year or two to turn B001 into a better candidate than the clock.
Whether IceCube source associations will be confirmed independently, which would raise B039 in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My own research (string theory, quantum gravity, cosmology) and my ties to Gross, Rubinstein and Van Riet do not touch any shortlisted candidate. As Secretary I have a procedural role in commissioning the expert reports, which is not a personal connection to any candidate. I note Kroll's Boulder year and Olsson's Tokyo fellowship; neither seems to me to prevent a vote on B007, but I leave that judgement to the chair.
